newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Britain, Vietnam make slim progress on boatpeople.
newsitem.headline: Britain, Vietnam make slim progress on boatpeople.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Friday he had discussed with his Vietnamese counterpart plans to empty Hong Kong's boatpeople camps, but indicated slim progress had been made.
Rifkind, who arrived in Hanoi on Friday, said he had received an encouraging response from Foreign Minister Nguyen Manh Cam to the concerns he had raised on the issue.
But he said Vietnam needed to help more if the problem was to be resolved by the middle of next year, when the British colony is due to be returned to Chinese rule.
"I am not despondent. I am not pessimistic. But I would not want to claim the problem has been resolved," he said. "We still have an outstanding problem. The ball is in their court."
Rifkind said Hanoi recognised the need to expedite the return process, but added that a problem remained over boatpeople whom Vietnam refuses to recognise as its own nationals.
In many cases these are ethnic-Chinese Vietnamese. Rifkind said it was impossible to estimate accurately how many people fell into this category.
Hong Kong is currently home to some 12,000 boatpeople, the last of a vast wave who fled their country in rickety boats following the end of the Vietnam War in 1975.
In October, the British colony repatriated some 1,700, the highest monthly total in years.

But concerned groups and others have warned that the final phase of the 20-year saga is likely to face problems with resistance from people who have held out against deportation, in some cases, for many years.
Hong Kong has a policy of detaining all boatpeople in vast refugee camps, pending a screening process aimed at determining claims to asylum.
Traditionally boatpeople have arrived in the colony seeking resettlement as a refugee in a third country.
But British officials say several hundred have arrived over the past year seeking illegal but lucrative employment before being caught and returned to Vietnam.
Rifkind, who has been in the region accompanying a royal visit, is due to meet Vietnam's top leaders on Saturday before leaving the communist country.
